introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2020. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Distinguish between the following pairs of terms:

(i) overland flow and base flow,

(ii) tropical rainforest and tropical monsoon climates.

(13 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Overland flow and base flow.**

(i) **Overland flow** is water that runs over the ground surface towards a stream channel. It occurs when rain falls faster than the soil can absorb it (rainfall intensity greater than infiltration capacity), or when the soil is already saturated, or on impermeable surfaces such as bare rock, baked soil and roofs or roads in towns. It is fast (minutes to hours), it reaches the river soon after the storm and it therefore produces the steep rising limb and high peak of a storm hydrograph. It is also the main agent of sheet wash and soil erosion. Flash floods in towns with many paved surfaces and in cleared catchments are a result of it.

**Base flow** is the part of river discharge that comes from groundwater. Water that has infiltrated and percolated down to the water table moves very slowly through permeable rock and soil (throughflow and groundwater flow) and seeps into the channel. It is slow, steady and long-lasting (weeks to months), it explains why rivers in permeable catchments keep flowing in dry weather, and on a hydrograph it forms the low, gently varying base level of the discharge, below the storm peak. Its volume depends on rock permeability and on how much the water table has been recharged.

| | Overland flow | Base flow |
|---|---|---|
| Source | Surface runoff of rain that cannot infiltrate | Groundwater seeping into the channel |
| Speed | Very rapid | Very slow |
| Effect on the hydrograph | Peak and steep rising limb | Low, steady base level |
| Favoured by | Heavy rain, impermeable or saturated ground, steep slopes, little vegetation | Permeable rocks and deep soils, gentle rain, dense vegetation |

(ii) **Tropical rainforest (equatorial) and tropical monsoon climates.** Both are hot, humid and found within the tropics, and both carry evergreen forest, but they differ in the distribution of rainfall.

| | Tropical rainforest climate | Tropical monsoon climate |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Close to the equator, about 5 degrees N and S (Congo Basin, Amazon Basin, south Cameroon plateau, Malaysia and Indonesia) | Coastal tropical lands exposed to a seasonal reversal of winds (west coast of Africa from Guinea to Cameroon, south and south-east Asia such as the Indian west coast, Bangladesh and Myanmar) |
| Temperature | High all year (about 26-28 degrees C) with a very small annual range (about 2-3 degrees C) | High, but a larger annual range than in the rainforest, and a fall in temperature in the wet season because of cloud and rain |
| Rainfall total | Very high, generally above 2 000 mm | Very high to extreme, often higher than in the rainforest (some Cameroon coastal stations get more than 3 000 mm) |
| Rainfall distribution | Well spread over the year, no real dry season; convectional rain almost every afternoon, with two slight maxima after the equinoxes | Strongly seasonal: most rain falls in the summer monsoon, when moist onshore winds blow from the ocean, and there is a short but definite dry season when the dry continental wind blows |
| Cause | The ITCZ and intense convection throughout the year | Seasonal shift of the ITCZ and the wind reversal between land and sea, with relief rainfall on exposed slopes |
| Vegetation | Dense, tall evergreen rainforest with several layers | Evergreen or semi-deciduous monsoon forest that can lose some leaves in the dry spell |

The key distinction is therefore the rainfall regime: evenly distributed in the rainforest, markedly seasonal in the monsoon climate.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Explain **three** reasons why temperatures fall with increase in height.

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Reasons why temperature falls with height.** Under normal conditions the air temperature decreases by about 6.5 degrees C for every 1 000 m of altitude (the normal or environmental lapse rate). Three main reasons explain this.

1. **The atmosphere is heated mainly from below.** Short-wave solar radiation passes through the clear air with little absorption and warms the ground. The ground then heats the air in contact with it by conduction and by long-wave (terrestrial) radiation. The farther the air is from this heat source, the cooler it is, so temperature decreases as one climbs away from the surface.

2. **Air becomes thinner with altitude.** Air density and pressure fall with height, so there are fewer gas molecules, less water vapour, less dust and less carbon dioxide to absorb and hold the heat given off by the ground (the greenhouse effect is weaker). High mountains therefore lose heat quickly, particularly at night when clear, thin air lets outgoing radiation escape.

3. **Adiabatic cooling of rising air.** When air rises up a slope or in a convection current, it moves into lower pressure and expands. Expansion uses up energy, so the air cools without any heat being lost to outside (adiabatic cooling): at the dry adiabatic lapse rate of about 10 degrees C per 1 000 m while the air is unsaturated, and at the saturated lapse rate of about 5 degrees C per 1 000 m after condensation has begun, because condensation releases latent heat.

Other contributing factors: high places are more exposed to wind, which removes heat, and snow and ice surfaces reflect a large part of incoming radiation back to space. **Example:** Mount Cameroon and Mount Kilimanjaro have cool or cold summits even though they are close to the equator, and permanent snow and ice are found on Kilimanjaro.
